org-design-conways-law-reverse-maneuver.core: Conway's Law means organisations ship their communication structure. Use the Inverse Conway Maneuver to design teams for the architecture you want, respect team cognitive load, define explicit team APIs, and keep teams long-lived so ownership and architecture stay coherent.

first_principles.problem: Ignoring Conway's Law produces accidental architectures and distributed monoliths shaped by org charts.

analogy.title: City districts and their roads
analogy.story: The way neighbourhoods are organised determines where roads go. Plan the neighbourhoods to get the road network you want.
analogy.breaks: Reorgs are disruptive and slow, so make deliberate, incremental changes.

example.title: Re-architecting through org design
example.outcome: org design used as an architecture tool.

check.q: How should you change an organisation to get a desired architecture?
check.a: Restructure teams to match the desired boundaries (Inverse Conway), with clear APIs and manageable cognitive load.

org-design-influence-without-authority.core: Influence without authority drives change through trust and persuasion: build social capital, map stakeholders and tailor messages, sell the problem before the solution (and co-create), and treat resistance as information to address.

first_principles.problem: Engineers responsible for org-wide change rarely have the authority to mandate it, and mandates breed resistance.
truths: People back solutions to problems they own.

analogy.title: A community organiser
analogy.story: No formal power, but trusted relationships, understanding of neighbours' needs, shared problems and patient negotiation create real change.
analogy.breaks: Influence takes longer than mandates, so plan for the time.

example.title: Driving an org-wide observability standard
example.outcome: large-scale change led without formal authority.

check.q: What's the foundation of influence without authority?
check.a: Social capital: trust built through reliable, helpful behaviour over time.

org-design-written-culture-narratives-rf.core: Written culture scales engineering thinking: narratives (Amazon's 6-pager) force complete reasoning, RFCs bring inclusive, recorded technical decisions, and strategy documents built on diagnosis, guiding policy and coherent actions replace fluff with real choices.

first_principles.problem: Spoken, slide-based or undocumented decisions are shallow, exclusive and quickly forgotten.

analogy.title: A constitution, laws and legislative records
analogy.story: Founding narratives, proposed bills open to debate and recorded decisions shape a society over time.
analogy.breaks: Writing culture fails if documents aren't read and discussed, so build the rituals around them.

example.title: An engineering org's writing system

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Decisions are clear, inclusive and remembered.

example.outcome: an organisation that thinks in writing.

check.q: How does a written culture help distributed teams?
check.a: Documents let everyone contribute and understand decisions asynchronously across time zones.

org-design-mentorship-sponsorship-ladder.core: Growing the team multiplies impact: mentor (advice) and sponsor (advocacy) deliberately and equitably, make growth transparent with career ladders, raise the bus factor through knowledge transfer, and plan succession for critical roles.

first_principles.problem: Teams that depend on heroes stagnate, lose knowledge and stall when people leave.

analogy.title: A sports academy
analogy.story: Coaches (mentors), scouts (sponsors), age-group levels (ladders), shared playbooks (knowledge) and a bench ready to step in (succession).
analogy.breaks: It takes time away from delivery, but it's an investment that pays back many times over.

example.title: A senior engineer's growth plan for the team
flow: Sponsor 1 for a cross-team lead role

check.q: Which practice directly reduces the risk of losing a critical expert?
check.a: Knowledge transfer (raising the bus factor) through pairing, documentation and shared on-call.

org-design-culture-safety-westrum.core: Culture is the invisible architecture of engineering: psychological safety lets people speak up, Westrum's generative culture lets information flow, just culture balances accountability with fairness, blameless postmortems put it into operation, and together they make a learning organisation.

first_principles.problem: Fearful, siloed or blame-heavy cultures hide problems and repeat failures, whatever the strategy.

analogy.title: A building's foundations
analogy.story: You don't see them, but every floor (strategy, process, technology) depends on them.
analogy.breaks: Culture change is slow, and leaders' daily behaviour matters far more than statements.

example.title: Measuring and improving culture

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Problems surface early and are fixed for good.

example.outcome: a culture that supports high performance.

check.q: Which Westrum culture type correlates with high software delivery performance?

org-design-team-topologies-flow.core: Team Topologies designs organisations for fast flow: map value streams, not just org charts, use four team types (mostly stream-aligned, supported by platform, enabling and complicated-subsystem teams), let platforms absorb cognitive load, and choose interaction modes deliberately.

first_principles.problem: Static org charts produce handoffs, overloaded teams and endless coordination.

analogy.title: A well-planned transport network
analogy.story: Express lines (stream-aligned), utilities and depots (platform), training centres (enabling) and specialist maintenance (complicated subsystem), with clear rules for connecting.
analogy.breaks: It's a model to adapt, not a rigid template.

example.title: Redesigning for flow
example.outcome: an organisation designed for delivery speed.

check.q: What are the three Team Topologies interaction modes?

org-design-change-management-satir-kotte.core: Change management handles the human physics of change: Satir's model predicts the emotional and performance dip, Kotter's 8 steps give leaders a roadmap from urgency to anchoring in culture, and combining them aligns leadership actions with what people experience.

first_principles.problem: Technically good changes fail because leaders ignore emotions, skip steps or declare victory too early.
truths: Large change needs a coalition and urgency.

analogy.title: Moving a family to a new city
analogy.story: Explain why (urgency), involve everyone (coalition), expect a rough first month (chaos), celebrate the first new friends (wins) and build new routines (anchor).
analogy.breaks: Models simplify. Adapt to your organisation's reality.

example.title: An observability platform rollout
flow: Embedded in templates; old tool retired

check.q: Why might a change be abandoned prematurely?
check.a: Leaders misread the normal Satir performance dip as failure and roll back before the improvement arrives.

org-design-hiring-bar-raising.core: Hiring is engineering the team: structured loops with competency rubrics predict performance, bar raisers protect standards against urgency, independent votes before debrief discussion reduce bias, and calibration keeps levels consistent.

first_principles.problem: Ad-hoc, biased and inconsistent hiring degrades team quality and fairness.

analogy.title: A rigorous admissions process
analogy.story: Clear criteria, independent reviewers, sealed scores and committee calibration keep standards fair.
analogy.breaks: Process must stay humane and timely, because candidates experience it too.

check.q: Name two practices that reduce bias in hiring decisions.
check.a: For example, structured rubric-based interviews and independent votes submitted before the debrief discussion.

org-design-budget-headcount-allocation.core: Engineering economics treats people as the biggest investment: work within the planning cycle, justify requests with ROI rather than burnout, allocate capacity across Run/Grow/Transform, respect Brooks's law, and request the role archetype that matches the real bottleneck.

first_principles.problem: Emotional, mistimed or misdirected headcount requests fail, and capacity gets consumed by maintenance.
truths: Hires are expensive and slow to ramp.

analogy.title: Managing a sports club's budget
analogy.story: Sign players during the transfer window, justify each by expected wins, balance squad roles and don't sign five strikers mid-match.
analogy.breaks: Budgets are political as well as financial, so build relationships with finance.

example.title: A successful planning season
example.outcome: engineering capacity managed like an investment portfolio.

check.a: Explicitly allocating engineering capacity across maintenance, product improvement and new strategic bets.

org-design-time-management-deep-work.core: Defending flow means managing time and energy for deep work: separate maker and manager schedules, practise deep work with distractions removed, use Pomodoro to beat procrastination, defragment the calendar, and match tasks to your energy curve.

first_principles.problem: Fragmented calendars, constant pings and poorly timed work starve engineers of the focus that hard problems need.
truths: Focus can be scheduled and trained.

analogy.title: A professional musician's practice routine
analogy.story: Long uninterrupted sessions, a quiet room, timed sets, a planned week and the hardest pieces when fresh.
analogy.breaks: Team responsibilities remain, so agree on norms rather than isolating yourself.

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Leadership duties met and hard problems solved.

check.q: What's the core enemy of deep work for engineers?
check.a: Context switching from fragmented calendars and constant interruptions.

org-design-remote-async-handbook.core: Remote and async culture is communication design: default to written, async work, keep a handbook as the single source of truth, design processes that don't need overlap, treat writing as the primary skill, and decide through RFCs recorded as ADRs.

first_principles.problem: Office habits moved onto video calls exclude time zones, fragment focus and lose decisions.
truths: Sync time is scarce across zones.

analogy.title: An international research collaboration
analogy.story: Shared papers, a lab manual, clear handoffs between labs, precise writing and formal records of conclusions.
analogy.breaks: Teams still need some sync time for connection and conflict resolution.

example.title: An async-first team week

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: A global team that rarely waits on each other.

example.outcome: distributed teams that work without waiting.

check.a: Defaulting to written, documented communication and decisions that don't need everyone online at once.

org-design-neurodiversity-inclusion.core: Neurodiversity is a hidden talent pool: brains run different 'operating systems' with spiky profiles of strengths and challenges. Inclusion means re-engineering interviews away from social performance, designing sensory- and socially-safe environments, communicating literally and making it safe to ask for support.

first_principles.problem: Processes built for one cognitive style exclude and burn out talented engineers.

analogy.title: Designing software for many platforms
analogy.story: Instead of forcing every device to behave like one, you build adaptable software that runs well on each.
analogy.breaks: Avoid stereotypes. Individuals vary widely, so always ask.

example.title: A neuroinclusive team
flow: Explicit tickets with definitions of done
example.outcome: an engineering culture that uses every kind of mind.

check.q: Name two practices that make engineering teams more neuroinclusive.
check.a: For example, sharing interview formats in advance and using explicit, literal communication with clear definitions of done.

org-design-tech-debt-quadrant.core: Technical debt is borrowed time that accrues interest. Fowler's quadrant (deliberate/inadvertent × reckless/prudent) separates strategic trade-offs from negligence and learning from skill gaps, so each type gets the right response, prioritised by interest cost.

first_principles.problem: Treating all 'messy code' the same leads to poor prioritisation and recurring reckless debt.

analogy.title: Personal finance counselling
analogy.story: Distinguish a planned mortgage from impulsive spending and from financial illiteracy, then treat each differently.
analogy.breaks: Some debt never needs repaying, if the code is rarely touched or about to be retired.

example.title: A quarterly debt strategy
flow: Policy: deliberate debt needs ticket + date

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Debt shrinks where it hurts, and less reckless debt appears.

check.q: What are the two axes of Fowler's technical debt quadrant?
check.a: Deliberate vs inadvertent, and reckless vs prudent.

org-design-wardley-mapping.core: Wardley Mapping gives strategic situational awareness: anchor on a user need, chain components by visibility, place them on evolution (genesis → commodity), and match investment to each stage, building differentiators and renting commodities, while watching for inertia and acting on what you see.

first_principles.problem: Strategy without a map of the landscape leads to building commodities and neglecting differentiation.

analogy.title: A military campaign map
analogy.story: Terrain, positions and movements shape which manoeuvres make sense.
analogy.breaks: Maps are subjective models, so their value is in the discussion and decisions they enable.

example.title: A platform strategy from a map
flow: Commodity: compute, K8s, logging → managed services
Custom: golden paths, policy engine → build

check.q: What's the 'golden rule' of Wardley Mapping?
check.a: Treat each component according to its evolution stage: explore genesis, build custom, buy products and rent commodities.

org-design-dreyfus-skill-acquisition.core: The Dreyfus model replaces tenure with skill stages per domain (novice, advanced beginner, competent, proficient, expert), explains why experts struggle to teach novices, and prescribes matching instruction and management style to each stage.

first_principles.problem: Tenure-based assumptions mismatch support to skill, frustrating experts and abandoning novices.

analogy.title: Martial arts belts per discipline
analogy.story: Black belt in judo, white belt in karate. Each discipline gets its own training approach.
analogy.breaks: It's a model, and real growth is messy and uneven.

example.title: A team skills matrix
flow: Map each person × skill to stage
example.outcome: skill development guided by how people really learn.

check.q: What's the key practical lesson of the Dreyfus model for managers?
check.a: Match the level of instruction and autonomy to the person's stage in each specific skill.

managing-vendor-relationships.core: Vendor management treats vendors as long-term dependencies: classify them as utility or partner, select with structured RFP bake-offs and real-data PoCs, negotiate exit terms before signing, and run the relationship actively with QBRs, usage tracking and credible alternatives.

first_principles.problem: Demo-driven selection and neglected relationships lead to lock-in, overpayment and poor support.

analogy.title: Choosing and managing a key supplier for a factory
analogy.story: Strategic vs commodity parts, trial runs, contracts with exit clauses and regular performance reviews.
analogy.breaks: Procurement and legal must be involved, because engineers shouldn't negotiate alone.

example.title: Selecting an observability partner

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: A strong partnership with leverage kept.

example.outcome: vendors that serve you, not trap you.

check.q: What's the most important time to negotiate vendor exit terms?
check.a: Before signing, when your leverage is greatest.
